at strikke.explanation: "At strikke" means "to knit". To mix it up with the other yarn craft, use "at hækle" (to crochet): "Jeg hækler et tæppe" (I crochet a blanket).

at stryge.explanation: "At stryge" means "to iron". To say you iron clothes, say: "Jeg stryger tøj" (I iron clothes). To say you stroke a pet, use the same verb: "Hun stryger katten" (She strokes the cat).

at stræbe.explanation: "At stræbe" means "to strive". To name the goal you strive for, use "efter" (after): "stræbe efter succes" (to strive for success). The adjective "stræbsom" (ambitious) comes from the same verb.

at strække.explanation: "At strække" means "to stretch". To say you stretch something out, say: "Han strækker armene" (He stretches his arms). To say you stretch your own body, add "sig" (oneself): "Katten strækker sig" (The cat stretches).

at strække sig.explanation: "At strække sig" means "to stretch". To say you stretch after a workout, say: "Han strækker sig efter træning" (He stretches after exercise). The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with who stretches: "vi strækker os" (we stretch).

at strø.explanation: "At strø" means "to sprinkle / scatter". To say someone spends money freely, add "om sig" (around oneself): "Han strør om sig med penge" (He throws money around).

at studere.explanation: "At studere" means "to study". To say what someone is studying to become, use "at læse til" (literally, to read for): "Hun læser til læge" (She is studying to be a doctor).

related.en: a study, a course of study

at styre.explanation: "At styre" means "to control / steer". To say you run a company, say: "Han styrer firmaet" (He runs the company).

at styrke.explanation: "At styrke" means "to strengthen". To say something made a friendship stronger, say: "Turen styrkede venskabet" (The trip strengthened the friendship).

at styrte.explanation: "At styrte" means "to rush / crash". To say you hurry somewhere, use it with no "ned" (down): "Jeg styrtede hjem" (I rushed home). To say something falls or crashes, add "ned": "Flyet styrtede ned" (The plane crashed).

at stå.explanation: "At stå" means "to stand". To say where something upright is, say: "Flasken står på bordet" (The bottle is on the table). To say what is written somewhere, say: "Der står et navn på døren" (There is a name on the door).

at stå af.explanation: "At stå af" means "to get off". To say you leave a train, say: "Hun står af toget i Aarhus" (She gets off the train in Aarhus). For a bike, use "at stige af" (to get off): "Hun stiger af cyklen" (She gets off the bike).

at stå for.explanation: "At stå for" means "to be in charge of". To say you handle a job, say: "Jeg står for maden" (I am in charge of the food). To ask what an abbreviation means, use the same words: "Hvad står DSB for?" (What does DSB stand for?)

at stå i kø.explanation: "At stå i kø" means "to stand in line". To say traffic is jammed, use "kø" (line) alone: "Der er kø på motorvejen" (There is a traffic jam on the highway).

at stå op.explanation: "At stå op" means "to get up", as in getting out of bed. It is built from "at stå" (to stand) and "op" (up). To say you stand up from a chair, use "at rejse sig" (to stand up): "Han rejser sig fra stolen" (He stands up from the chair).

at stå på ski.explanation: "At stå på ski" means "to ski". Literally, it is "to stand on skis". To say you water ski, use "vandski" (water ski) in place of "ski": "Jeg står på vandski" (I water ski).

at støde på.explanation: "At støde på" means "to come across". To say you meet a person by chance, say: "Jeg stødte på min gamle lærer i byen" (I came across my old teacher in town). To say you face a difficulty, say: "Vi stødte på modstand" (We met resistance).

at stønne.explanation: "At stønne" means "to groan". To name what you groan about, use "over" (about): "stønne over varmen" (to groan about the heat).

at støtte.explanation: "At støtte" means "to support". To say you back a project, say: "Vi støtter projektet" (We support the project). To say you lean on something, add "sig til" (oneself on): "Han støttede sig til væggen" (He leaned on the wall).

at støve af.explanation: "At støve af" means "to dust". To say what you dust, put the things before "af" (off): "Jeg støver hylderne af" (I dust the shelves). To say you refresh an old skill, say: "støve sit fransk af" (to dust off your French).

at støvsuge.explanation: "At støvsuge" means "to vacuum". It is built from "støv" (dust) and "at suge" (to suck), and the machine is "en støvsuger" (a vacuum cleaner).

at suge.explanation: "At suge" means "to suck". To name what you suck on, use "på" (on): "Babyen suger på sutten" (The baby sucks on the pacifier). The noun "en støvsuger" (a vacuum cleaner) is built from "støv" (dust) and this verb.

at sukke.explanation: "At sukke" means "to sigh". To name what you sigh about, use "over" (about): "Hun sukker over vejret" (She sighs about the weather). The noun is "et suk" (a sigh).

at sulte.explanation: "At sulte" means "to starve". To say you are simply hungry, use "sulten" (hungry) instead: "Jeg er sulten" (I am hungry).

at summe.explanation: "At summe" means "to buzz". To say a place is full of life, say: "Byen summer af liv" (The city buzzes with life). To hum a tune, use "at nynne" (to hum): "Hun nynner en melodi" (She hums a tune).
